bib.title: Harness as a Language: A Minimalist Agent Framework With Maximal Expressivity

legacy_report:
COVERAGE: all 26 pages read (92,618 chars extracted). Body pp.1-10, references p.11+, appendices A-F (hooks, protocol, task details, tables 3-4, prompts) skimmed or read for the parts below. The extraction was clean. There were no embedded instructions.

SOURCE: "Harness as a Language: A Minimalist Agent Framework With Maximal Expressivity". Zhening Li, Joshua Liu, Mateja Vukelic, Nicole Shen, Supriya Lall, Alex Zhang, Omar Khattab, Amitayush Thakur, Jonathan Light, Armando Solar-Lezama. Most authors are at MIT CSAIL; Thakur and Light are independent researchers. It is an arXiv preprint (cs.AI), v2, 30 Sep 2026. The PDF gives the id as 2609.26891. Code: github.com/jaz-lang/jaz and jaz-evals.

MAIN CLAIM: A minimal "invoke" agent loop can do what memory systems and self-improvement harnesses do, using prompting alone. In this loop the LLM writes code, subagents are recursive calls, and all inputs and the REPL history are variables in the REPL. The paper builds the JAZ framework around this. For long recall, the agent hands off to a subagent when its context fills and passes the whole history by reference (the paper's "tail-recursive delegation"). It then searches that raw history with code. No memory store or memory tool is involved. This supports the "searching the raw record" side of your section.

HEADLINE NUMBERS (all from Table 1 on p.7 and Table 2 on p.9; mean ± standard error)
1. StuLife far-recall subset (207 of 939 graded tasks, from an ordered 1284-task sequence; GPT-5.4 nano (high); 3 runs).
   - JAZ invoke: 69.9±1.8 pass, $18.3 per run.
   - Letta (MemGPT) v0.16.8: 61.8±2.3 pass, $42.1.
   - CodeAct+subagents, JAZ reimplementation: 32.0±2.3 pass.
   - CodeAct per task, no memory: 24.8±0.6 pass.
   - The abstract's "8% at half its cost" matches this gap (about 8 points) and the cost ratio.
2. StuLife, all 939 graded tasks. JAZ invoke 72.6±0.1 pass, against Letta 70.9±0.5 and CodeAct+subagents 60.0±1.1. The gap over Letta is small.
3. AppWorld test-challenge (417 tasks, shuffled with seed 42). The solver is GPT-5.4 nano and the meta-agent is GPT-5.4. n=6 runs for self-improving methods, n=3 for the others.
   - Task goal completion (TGC): JAZ invoke 74.2±2.1, CodeAct+subagents 71.1±1.3, ACE 69.9±1.4, per-task CodeAct 67.5±1.2.
   - Cost: $20.9 for JAZ invoke against $30.6 for ACE.
   - The margins are about one to two standard errors. JAZ invoke's TGC error is ±2.1.
4. Failure case (task 1282/1284): the needed lecture came from task 785, 497 tasks earlier. JAZ invoke solved it in 3 of 3 runs, Letta once, CodeAct+subagents zero times.

QUOTES
- p.7: "Takeaway 1: (long-horizon version) When everything the agent sees in its context is in REPL variables, the agent can pass them by reference to a subagent in scenarios that need it (e.g., tail-recursive delegation). This is more reliable than copying their contents by hand."
- p.8: Letta's "conversation_search" returned "the quiz question itself, or earlier messages about similarly named but different protocols. In this scenario where the agent needs exact substring matching, the only tool Letta had (conversation_search) did not support it."
- p.5, related work: "In JAZ, we showed that full programmatic access to a variable __history__ is sufficient for memory retrieval."

LIMITS
- Only two benchmarks (StuLife, AppWorld) and only GPT-5.4 nano as the solver. Larger or other models are not tested.
- It does not test memory that carries over between separate sessions. StuLife is one long episode and the history is raw and lossless. Nothing is distilled, updated or forgotten, and there is no staleness or contradiction handling. This is not a test of "designed memory" in the sense of distilled facts.
- Recall here is exact-match search over history that is still kept in full. Cost and latency may grow with history length. Depth reached 70 delegations in one run.
- Letta caveats (p.17). The SQL search backend returned mostly empty results, so Turbopuffer hybrid search was used. Tasks had to be sent as user messages, because tool outputs are not searchable in Letta. Most Letta prompts fell into infinite loops, and the authors report only the one prompt that avoided this. This is the authors' own setup, so the comparison may favour JAZ. Letta also has no standard error on the all-tasks line shown here beyond ±0.5.
- The smolagents baseline underperforms mainly through a prompt defect, which is why the authors reimplemented CodeAct in JAZ.
- ACE learning was restricted to the first 42 tasks (10%) for cost.
- The "prompt-only" claim holds under the authors' own restrictions (Appendix C.1). There is no separate Limitations section.
- Autonomous prompts are tuned per method, but kept task-agnostic.

BUILDS ON: ReAct (Yao et al.); CodeAct (Wang et al. [2]); Recursive Language Models (RLM, Zhang/Khattab [5]); smolagents [4]; MemGPT/Letta [7]; ACE, Agentic Context Engineering [9]; StuLife [6]; AppWorld [8]; compaction [10,11]; Chroma Context-1 [12]. I did not check the full reference list for years or venues, so confirm them against p.11+ before citing.

FIGURE CANDIDATE: Figure 1 (p.1-2) shows invoke as a function whose body the LLM writes, with all inputs and history as variables. The p.1 scatter plots of cost against pass rate are the other candidate: StuLife far-recall, with and without a memory system, and AppWorld. For the memory section, use the StuLife far-recall plot.
